entry.title: No warnings are in force. Halloween stays dry and mild, then a strong high over Scotland brings a week of calm, foggy, grey weather, with rain returning around 9-10 November. Overhead, the polar vortex is forecast to reverse around 5 November in every ECMWF and Canadian ensemble member.
entry.content:
At 08:50 UTC Edinburgh Airport had 9 °C (dew point 8 °C), a light westerly, clear skies (CAVOK) and 1030 hPa. There was fog nearby at 07:20 and a low of 7 °C, matching the hourly guidance. Halloween is dry and mild, near 14.5 °C. The weak front tonight now gives no measurable rain, just a gustier south-westerly and cloud. Sunday is fresher and bright. From Monday a 1033-1039 hPa high sits over Scotland, centred over the north-east by Thursday 5 November in ECMWF and ICON. That means calm, often foggy or grey days near 10 °C, a chilly first half of Monday night, and possible drizzle from low cloud on 3 and 6 November. Around 8-10 November the high drifts towards Scandinavia and Atlantic lows push in from the south-west: ECMWF HRES has a deep low south-west of Ireland by 10 November, and the ensembles have a more than 1 mm chance of 45-57% a day on 10-13 November. In the stratosphere the 60°N 10 hPa wind is 12.3 m/s, just above NASA's record low for the date (11.3 m/s). Every ECMWF ENS and GEPS member and 90% of GEFS reverse it to easterly around 5 November. On the 100 hPa polar cap the event is deep (+1.8 sd now, peaks +2.1 to +2.4 sd); on the 50 hPa wind it is not (westerly throughout).

What changed: Short range unchanged: dry and mild to Halloween, then a foggy high on 2-6 November. Yesterday verified at 15 °C. Changes since the last analysis: - Halloween's spot of drizzle has gone; the hourly guidance is dry. - The high is now centred over north-east Scotland on 5 November in ECMWF and ICON. - Drizzle risk on 6 November has risen in AIFS ENS, GEM ENS and AIGEFS. - Medium range: ECMWF HRES and JMA now bring a deep Atlantic low south-west of Ireland by 10 November, so the wet, breezy turn around 9-10 November is firmer, with south-easterlies rather than AIFS's cold north-westerly. - Snow: ECMWF ENS snow members fell from 2-4% to 0%. - Upwind cold eased: Stockholm's share of members at -8 °C is down from 14% to 8%, Oslo from 6% to 4%. - ECMWF extended products updated to the 30 October run: Atlantic Ridge on 8-14 November, NAO+ largest on 17-24 November, and blocking stronger in early December (about 40% against 26-35% before). Stratosphere: - NASA's climatology loaded this run: the 10 hPa wind is just above the record low for the date, and the 50 hPa wind is at its record low. - GEFS reversal share rose from 77% to 90% in the new 00Z run. - AIFS ENS fell from 73% to 51%, and the AIFS deterministic minimum rose to 3.6 m/s. - ECMWF ENS is still 100%, slightly deeper (mean -4.0 m/s, lowest member -10.0 m/s), but recovers a little sooner (39% easterly on 14 November). - ECMWF HRES now recovers to +3.4 m/s by 14 November. - The 50 hPa wind stays westerly everywhere (AIGEFS easterly share down from 23% to 3%). - The 100 hPa cap is still deep. GFS surface coupling is slightly stronger again (1000 hPa cap +0.86 sd on 7 November, against +0.5-0.6).

SSW risk: high. A major reversal in the first week of November is almost unprecedented. It looks short at 10 hPa, roughly 5-14 November, but it is deep on the 100 hPa polar cap. The troposphere is already going that way: GEFS forecasts the AO at -1.4 and the NAO at about -1 by 10-13 November. Much of that comes from the same Ural-Scandinavian block that drove the wave pulse, not from a downward response. About two thirds of events like this couple down, typically 1-3 weeks later. That puts Edinburgh's window for extra blocking and colder interludes at about mid-November to early December, and ECMWF's blocking regime rising to about 40% on 3-7 December fits that. Several things temper it: - the 50 hPa wind stays westerly; - the QBO is westerly (+12.9 m/s at 30 hPa); - the wave driving collapses after 8 November; - ECMWF rebuilds the vortex to above normal (about 42 m/s) by mid-December, which would favour mild, wet westerlies later in December; - the cold source upwind is thin: at most 8% of ECMWF members have -8 °C at 850 hPa over Stockholm or Oslo by 14 November, with almost no snow cover; - the North Sea is +1.1 °C above its 1991-2020 normal (58% of cells above +1 °C, OISST). For the city, a blocked spell in the next month most likely means frost, fog and raw, grey easterlies, or a chilly north-westerly with snow showers on the Pentlands, rather than lowland snow.

entry.title: No warnings are in force. Halloween stays dry and mild, then a strong high brings fog, grey days and a chilly night into Monday 2 November. Rain returns from about 8-9 November. Meanwhile the polar vortex reverses around 4-5 November in every ECMWF and Canadian ensemble member.
entry.content:
At 17:50 UTC Edinburgh Airport had 11 °C (dew point 8 °C), a light westerly, clear skies (CAVOK) and 1027 hPa, after a high of 15 °C today. That is a degree above most model highs, consistent with the models' cool bias here. Halloween is dry and mild, about 14 °C. A very weak front brings at most a spot of drizzle around 22:00, then a fresher, bright Sunday. A 1040-1042 hPa high then settles over or just west of Scotland from 2 November. Expect calm, often foggy or grey days near 10 °C, with the clear night into Monday 2 November the coldest (about 2 °C, ground frost in hollows). From about 7-9 November the models part. ECMWF ENS and GEFS means bring Atlantic lows to the south-west and rain. The 12Z machine-learning AIFS run turns it into a chilly north-westerly, and GEM into a mild southerly. In the stratosphere the 60°N 10 hPa wind is 13.1 m/s, weaker than 9 years in 10 and near the record low for the date. Members reversing to easterly: 100% of ECMWF ENS and GEPS, 77% of GEFS and 73% of AIFS ENS. On the 100 hPa polar cap the event is deep (+1.8 sd now, peaks +2.2 to +2.4 sd), but the 50 hPa wind stays westerly. GEFS now takes the NAO to about -1 by 10-14 November.

What changed: Short range unchanged: dry and mild to Halloween, then a foggy high on 2-6 November. Today verified at 15 °C, slightly above my 14.5 °C. The hourly guidance now puts Halloween's drizzle near 22:00. Several things changed in the newer runs: - NAO and AO: the GEFS NAO is markedly more negative (-0.9 to -1.06 on 10-13 November with 90% of members negative, against -0.3 to -0.4). The AO now sits at about -1.4 through 6-13 November. - Medium range: the 12Z AIFS deterministic run turns a chilly north-westerly on 9 November (850 hPa -1 °C), while GEM 12Z goes mild southerly; the ECMWF ENS and GEFS means keep a south-westerly Atlantic low. Spread after day 7 has widened. - Met Office: its text now hints that lows track further south than normal in the second half of November. - Upwind cold: building slightly, with Stockholm up from 8% to 10-14% of members at -8 °C and Helsinki 18-25%. Stratosphere: - Reversal is still near-certain in ECMWF ENS and GEPS (100%), but fewer GEFS members reverse (94% down to 77%) and fewer AIFS ENS members (78% down to 73%). - The AIFS deterministic minimum is now 1.2 m/s. - ECMWF ENS is deeper (mean -3.7 m/s, lowest member -9.6 m/s). - 50 hPa easterly shares dropped (GEFS 6% to 0%, AIGEFS 52% to 23%). - The 100 hPa cap is still deep, but GFS's surface coupling weakened (1000 hPa cap +0.6 sd, against +1.4).

SSW risk: high. A major reversal at 10 hPa in the first week of November is close to unprecedented. It looks short, roughly 4-13 November in most ensembles (longer in GEPS and ECMWF ENS), but it is deep on the 100 hPa polar cap. That is consistent with the GEFS AO already forecast at -1.4 and the NAO at about -1 by 10-13 November. About two thirds of events like this reach the troposphere, typically 1-3 weeks later, which puts Edinburgh's window for blocking and colder interludes at roughly mid-November to early December. Several things temper it: - the 50 hPa wind stays westerly in the physics ensembles; - the QBO is westerly (+12.9 m/s at 30 hPa); - wave forcing collapses after 8 November; - today's runs couple less strongly to the surface (GFS 1000 hPa cap +0.6 sd, AIFS 500 hPa cap negative); - ECMWF rebuilds the vortex to above normal by mid-December. The cold source is also thin. At most 6-14% of ECMWF members have -8 °C at 850 hPa over Oslo or Stockholm by 13 November, with almost no snow cover, and the North Sea is warmer than normal. For the city, a blocked spell in the next month most likely means frost, fog and raw grey days, or a chilly north-westerly with snow showers on the Pentlands. Lowland snow would need a real cold pool over Scandinavia first.

entry.title: No warnings are in force: it stays dry and mild through Halloween, then high pressure brings fog, grey days and chilly nights to about 6 November before Atlantic rain returns from around 8-9 November, while the polar vortex reverses in nearly every ensemble member around 4-6 November.
entry.content:
At 08:50 UTC the airport had 7 °C (dew point 7 °C), near calm, 1026 hPa and only a few clouds at 2,300 ft. The hourly guidance is a couple of degrees too warm for the moment, but the forecast highs still stand. Today and Halloween are dry and mild at about 14-14.5 °C. A weak front clears through Halloween night with no more than a spot of drizzle around 20:00-21:00, followed by a fresher Sunday. A 1036-1040 hPa high then settles over Scotland from 2 November, bringing calm, often grey or foggy days near 10 °C. The clear night into Monday 2 November is the coldest, about 2 °C at the airport with ground frost in hollows; later nights are 4-6 °C under cloud. This morning's ECMWF run holds the high over Scotland to about 6 November, then moves it to Scandinavia with an Atlantic low to the south-west by 9 November, so rain and stronger south to south-easterly winds return from about 8-9 November. In the stratosphere the 60°N 10 hPa wind is 13.2 m/s, weaker than 9 years in 10 for the date and near the record low (11.0-11.4 m/s). It reverses in 100% of ECMWF ENS and GEPS members, 94% of GEFS and 78% of the machine-learning AIFS ENS. The event is deep on the 100 hPa polar-cap height (+1.8 sd now, peaking at +2.2 to +2.6 sd) but stays westerly at 50 hPa in almost every physics-ensemble member.

What changed: The short range is unchanged: dry and mild to Halloween (highs 14-14.5 °C), a very weak front on Halloween night, then a foggy high on 2-6 November. The hourly guidance now puts the front's drizzle on Halloween evening rather than early Sunday. ECMWF HRES holds the high over Scotland a little longer (1038-1039 hPa on 6 November), then moves it to Scandinavia with a 993 hPa Atlantic low to the south-west by 9 November. The ECMWF ENS and AIFS ENS means now agree on that south-westerly low and eastern high, so I lean towards southerlies and rain from about 8-9 November rather than a north-westerly edge. ECMWF ENS frost risk for 9-12 November drops from 18% to 4% or less, while the GFS 18Z run remains the cold north-easterly outlier around 8 November. The ECMWF extended products are unchanged (still the 29 October run). Simon Lee's newer index (28 October) keeps a weak NAO- lean through late November, at odds with ECMWF's NAO+ probabilities. In the stratosphere the reversal is still near-certain and slightly more widespread: GEFS rises from 84% to 94% of members and AIFS ENS from 69% to 78%, while ECMWF ENS and GEPS stay at 100%. ECMWF HRES now reverses deeper and longer (-4.8 m/s on 11 November, still easterly on 13 November); the AIFS deterministic run still does not reverse (weakest 0.3 m/s). The lower stratosphere is mixed. Physics ensembles still have only 2-6% of members easterly at 50 hPa and the GFS section now stops the easterlies at 30 hPa, but the machine-learning AIGEFS rises from 32% to 52% easterly at 50 hPa. The 100 hPa cap remains deep (ensemble peaks +2.2 to +2.6 sd), though GEFS now recovers fastest (35% of members above +1 sd by 13 November).

SSW risk: high. A major reversal at 10 hPa this early in November is close to unprecedented. It looks fairly short, about 4-13 November in most ensembles, but it is deep on the 100 hPa polar cap, which is why the GEFS AO is forecast negative from 2 November. About two thirds of events like this reach the troposphere, typically 1-3 weeks later, which puts Edinburgh's window for blocking and colder spells at roughly mid-November to early December. So far the ECMWF extended run shows little of that before about 30 November: it has an Atlantic Ridge, then NAO+ westerlies for 15-25 November, with blocking back to 26-35% from 2-8 December and a Greenland high on 7-14 December. That timing fits a lagged response. GFS couples it far more strongly and sooner. Several things argue against lasting cold. The 50 hPa wind stays westerly in the physics ensembles, the QBO is westerly (+12.9 m/s at 30 hPa) and the wave forcing eases after about 8 November. ECMWF rebuilds the vortex to above normal by mid-December, and there is no cold pool upwind: Oslo has 6% of members at -8 °C at 850 hPa and Copenhagen 2% by 13 November, with no snow cover. The North Sea is also about 1.1 °C warmer than normal. For the city, any blocked spell in the next month means frost, fog and raw grey days, with snow mainly on the Pentlands unless a real cold pool first builds over Scandinavia.

About two thirds of events like this couple to the surface, typically 1-3 weeks later, so Edinburgh's window for colder, blocked weather is roughly mid-November to mid-December. The newest ECMWF extended run shows little of that response before about 30 November: it has NAO+ westerlies for 14-25 November, then blocking back to 25-35% around 30 November-8 December and a Greenland high on 7-14 December. That timing fits a lagged response. GFS couples it far more strongly and sooner. Against lasting cold: the 50 hPa wind stays westerly, the QBO is westerly, the wave forcing dies off after about 8 November, ECMWF rebuilds the vortex to above normal by mid-December, and there is no cold source upwind. Oslo has only 14-24% of members at -5 °C at 850 hPa and 0-6% at -8 °C by 8-13 November, with no snow cover in Scandinavia, and the North Sea is 1.1 °C warm. For the city that means frost and cold nights in any blocked spell, with snow mainly on the Pentlands unless a real cold pool builds over Scandinavia first.

Lying snow in Edinburgh needs a proper northerly or easterly, and a North Sea about 1 °C above normal makes it more marginal at the coast. Several things argue against a long freeze: the 50 hPa wind mostly stays westerly, the QBO is westerly (+12.9 m/s), the heat flux returns to normal after about 9 November, and ECMWF rebuilds the vortex above normal by December. So I expect one or two colder interludes rather than a lasting cold spell, with mild westerlies returning in between.

entry.title: No warnings are in force. After a mild, mostly dry end to October, a very strong high (about 1040 hPa over Scotland) brings a dry, calm and often foggy spell with chilly nights from 2 to about 7 November. Above it, nearly every physics ensemble now reverses the polar vortex around 4-10 November.
entry.content:
At 08:50 Edinburgh Airport had 11 °C (dew point 9 °C), a south-westerly of 24 km/h, 1013 hPa and only a few clouds; overnight rain has cleared and yesterday's warning has expired. Today stays dry and breezy, with gusts of 40-45 km/h until about 16:00. Thursday and Friday are dry and mild at 13-15 °C. A weak front brings a 20-30% chance of light rain on Saturday evening and night, so guising may be damp in places. From Sunday a 1039-1042 hPa high settles over Scotland, giving dry, grey or foggy days near 10 °C and nights of 2-5 °C, colder in hollows; it starts to erode around 7-9 November, when the ensembles turn colder and more changeable. In the stratosphere the 60°N vortex is already weak (16.5 m/s, between the 10th and 30th percentile) and heads well below its record low for the date. 94% of ECMWF ENS members reverse at 10 hPa, along with 100% of GEPS, 68% of GEFS and 49% of the machine-learning AIFS ENS. The 100 hPa polar cap reaches +2.2 to +3.0 sd while the 50 hPa wind mostly stays westerly, so the cap measure calls the event deep and the 50 hPa wind calls it shallow.

What changed: Yesterday's yellow wind warning has expired and no warnings are in force. Saturday's front is weaker and later: the chance of more than 1 mm is now about 20-27%, down from 40-50%, and it now falls on the evening and night of 31 October into 1 November, so the Halloween evening could be drizzly rather than dry. The block is unchanged and slightly stronger (ECMWF 1042 hPa over Scotland on 2 November). In the ECMWF regimes it erodes a little sooner: blocking is about 25-30% by 5-6 November (it was 49% on 7 November), and the Atlantic Ridge now dominates 5-9 November at 50-55% (it was 35-39%). The early-December blocking signal has faded: NAO+ now leads at 31-35%, against blocking at 20-25%, where blocking was 31-43% before. The AO is forecast much more negative: -1.3 on 3-5 November, where it was -0.3 to -0.4 on 7-10 November. At the point, GEFS now turns colder after 8 November (mean 850 hPa below 0 °C), with snow in 10-13% of GEFS members on 10-11 November, while the GEM ENS cold tail has shrunk (10th percentile about -3 °C, was -8 °C). In the stratosphere the vortex has already fallen to 16.5 m/s (from 20 m/s), and the reversal odds are up again: ECMWF ENS 94% (was 47%), AIFS ENS 49% (was 22%), GEFS 68% (was 65%) and GEPS 100%. GFS now clearly reverses (-2.2 m/s from 4 November) and ECMWF HRES goes deeper (-3.1 m/s), while deterministic AIFS falls to 1.4 m/s but stays westerly. At 50 hPa, 33% of ECMWF ENS (was 12%), 23% of GEFS (was 0%) and 52% of AIGEFS (was 32%) members now reverse. The 100 hPa cap is still +2.2 to +3.0 sd, but the GFS section now gives only +0.5 to +0.8 sd at the surface (it was +1 sd). The vortex now ends displaced towards the North Atlantic and Scandinavia by 12-13 November. The ECMWF 46-day mean now bottoms near 1 m/s (was 3.5-4 m/s). The SEAS5 November point is now 6.3 °C with 53% of members milder (was 6.6 °C and 57%). The seasonal tilt is otherwise unchanged: mild and wet early, with a weak cold tilt in February.

SSW risk: high. A major SSW in early November would be almost unprecedented; the vortex will be record-weak for the date whether or not every model reverses. The 10 hPa reversal looks short, a few days to a week near 0 to -5 m/s around 4-11 November, followed by a fairly quick recovery. The high polar cap already reaches 100 hPa (+2 to +3 sd), which is why GEFS takes the AO to -1.3 on 3-5 November. Part of that is the tropospheric block itself. About two thirds of events couple down, typically 1-3 weeks later, which makes Edinburgh's window for colder, blocked spells roughly mid-November to early December. The first sign may be a colder north-westerly around 9-13 November, as the displaced vortex lobe drifts towards Greenland and Scandinavia. For the city that mostly means more frosts and cold nights, with snow on the Pentlands and higher ground. Lying snow in the city needs a proper northerly or easterly, made more marginal by a North Sea about 1 °C above normal. Several things argue against a long cold spell: the 50 hPa wind stays mostly westerly, the QBO is westerly (+12.9 m/s), the heat flux returns to normal after about 8 November, and ECMWF rebuilds the vortex above normal by early December. ECMWF's regimes also lean slightly NAO+ into December. So I expect one or two colder interludes rather than a lasting freeze, with mild westerlies returning for parts of December.

entry.title: A Met Office yellow wind warning runs until 21:00 today, with gusts near 80 km/h. High pressure then brings a mostly dry, calm and often foggy spell from Thursday to about 7 November. Meanwhile most ensembles now reverse the polar vortex briefly around 4-9 November.
entry.content:

The biggest change is in the stratosphere, so the SSW risk rises from medium to high. Reversal odds are up: GEFS 65% (was 39%), ECMWF ENS 47% in the Open-Meteo data (was 35%) and 86% on severe-weather.eu (was 52%), GEPS 100% (was 86%) and AIFS ENS 22-35% (was 18-24%). GFS now reaches 0 m/s (it was 2 m/s), and deterministic AIFS falls to 6.9 m/s (was 10.4). At 50 hPa, 12% of ECMWF ENS members and 32% of AIGEFS members now reverse (were 2% and 16%). The 100 hPa polar cap stays at +2 to +3 sd, and the GFS section now carries +1 sd to the surface on 3-9 Nov. The AER post used is new (26 Oct) and supports a late-November and December impact. The seasonal tilt is unchanged: mild and wet early, a weak cold tilt in February.

SSW risk: high. An early-November major SSW would be almost unprecedented. Even without a full reversal the vortex will be record-weak for the date. The 10 hPa reversal looks brief, a few days near 0 to -5 m/s around 4-10 Nov. The high polar cap already reaches 100 hPa and the surface, which is why the AO is forecast to turn negative on 6-10 Nov. About two thirds of events couple down, typically 1-3 weeks later. That makes Edinburgh's window for colder, blocked spells roughly mid-November to early December. It fits AER's expectation of late-November and December impacts and ECMWF's returning blocking (31-43%) in early December. For the city that mainly means more frost and cold nights, and snow on the Pentlands and higher ground; lying snow in the city needs a proper northerly or easterly outbreak, made more marginal by a North Sea 1 °C above normal. Four things argue against a long cold spell. The vortex ends up displaced towards the North Atlantic rather than split, the 50 hPa wind stays mostly westerly, the QBO is westerly, and ECMWF's 46-day run rebuilds the vortex above normal by December. entry.title: A Met Office yellow wind warning covers Edinburgh from 03:00 to 21:00 on Tuesday 27 Oct, with gusts of 65-80 km/h; the airport was already gusting 65 km/h before 23:00. From Thursday a strong high brings a long, dry, calm and often foggy spell to about 8 November. Meanwhile the polar vortex weakens far below its record low for the date, with about a 35-50% chance of a brief reversal around 4-10 Nov.
entry.content:
At 22:50 Edinburgh Airport was 17 °C with a gusty south-south-westerly (44 km/h, gusting 65 km/h) and 985 hPa, ahead of tonight's cold front. That is very mild and already windy, before the warning period starts. The front crosses with a burst of rain around 02:00-04:00, and temperatures drop to about 10-11 °C by dawn. Tuesday is then bright, squally and showery, with gusts of 65-80 km/h, strongest about 07:00-14:00. Wednesday has more rain in the small hours, and from Thursday high pressure takes charge. A weakening front on Friday and Saturday (30-31 Oct) is the only interruption, and the ECMWF run alone makes Halloween wet. From 1 Nov a 1035-1042 hPa high over Scotland and the North Sea gives dry, grey, calm days with fog and frosty nights in rural spots. There is no snow risk this week, and only a few percent of ensemble members bring hill snow by 9-11 Nov. In the stratosphere, the physics ensembles drive the 60°N 10 hPa wind far below the 1979-2026 record minimum. ECMWF ENS, GEFS and the Canadian GEPS give 35-86% of members a brief reversal around 4-10 Nov, against 18-24% in the machine-learning AIFS ENS. The 100 hPa polar-cap height reaches +2 to +2.8 standard deviations (sd) while the 50 hPa wind stays westerly. If it couples down, the odds of colder, blocked spells rise for mid-November to early December, but a strong vortex recovery is forecast by early December.

What changed: The short range played out as expected. Rain came around midday Monday, the airport reached 17 °C by late evening, and gusts hit 65 km/h before the yellow wind warning (03:00-21:00 Tue) even started. Tuesday's hourly gust peak is now about 79 km/h around 11:00, slightly earlier than before. The ECMWF HRES now makes Saturday 31 Oct wet (11.5 mm), raising the Halloween rain risk to medium, though most models stay drier. The block and its timing are unchanged, but ECMWF regime blocking fades a little faster: 38% on 8 Nov against 49% in the previous run. ECMWF's 2 Nov high is now even stronger at 1042 hPa. In the stratosphere, GFS no longer reverses the vortex: its minimum is about 2 m/s, where the previous run reached -5 m/s. The ensembles moved: ECMWF ENS is 35% in the Open-Meteo series (was 51%) but 52% on severe-weather.eu (was 40%), GEFS 39% (was 35%) and AIFS ENS 18-24% (was 12-14%). The new Canadian GEPS is the most disturbed, with 86% of members reversing. New polar-cap height data show the 100 hPa cap at +2 to +2.8 sd, with all members of four ensembles above +1 sd, so the event counts as deep by that measure even though the 50 hPa wind stays westerly. SSW risk stays medium. The SEAS5 November point is slightly milder (6.6 °C) and drier (65 mm) than last time. The winter tilt is unchanged: mild and wet early, a weak cold tilt in February.

SSW risk: medium. An early-November reversal would be almost unprecedented, and even without one the vortex will be record-weak for the date. The event looks brief, a few days at 0 to -5 m/s at 10 hPa, with the 50 hPa wind staying westerly. The high polar cap down to 100-500 hPa is largely concurrent with the tropospheric block, which is why the AO is forecast to turn negative on 6-10 Nov. If it couples further, as about two thirds of major events do 1-3 weeks later, Edinburgh's window is roughly 12 Nov to early December. That fits ECMWF's blocking returning to 31-43% and NAO- at 14-24% in early December. For the city it mainly means more frost, cold nights, and snow on the Pentlands and higher ground; lying snow in the city would need a proper northerly or easterly outbreak. Two things argue against a lasting effect. The vortex ends up displaced towards Greenland and the Atlantic, which tends to feed the jet near the UK. And the westerly QBO plus the strong ECMWF rebuild to above normal by December point to a fast recovery and mild, wet westerlies for much of December. The record El Niño keeps open a second, mid-to-late-winter weakening and a colder February.

entry.title: A Met Office yellow wind warning covers Edinburgh from 03:00 to 21:00 on Tuesday 27 Oct, with gusts of about 65-80 km/h peaking around midday. After a very mild, wet Monday, a strong dry high takes over from Thursday into the second week of November, while the polar vortex heads for record weakness and has roughly a 1-in-3 chance of a brief reversal around 4-10 Nov.
entry.content:
At 08:50 Edinburgh Airport was dry and cloudy, 9 °C with a light southerly and 1001 hPa, so the rain has not arrived yet. Rain spreads in from about 11:00, heaviest 13:00-15:00 (about 4 mm). Very mild air then lifts temperatures to about 15 °C by 18:00, and the south-westerly strengthens through the evening, with gusts of 65-75 km/h by 22:00-midnight. Tuesday's cold front brings rain in the small hours and then a bright, squally westerly under a yellow wind warning (03:00-21:00), with gusts of about 65-80 km/h, strongest late morning to mid-afternoon, and showers. From Thursday high pressure builds and becomes dominant from about 1 Nov to 8 Nov. That means mostly dry, often grey weather with light winds, and fog and frost on clear nights, with only a weakening front on 30-31 Oct to spoil it. There is no snow risk this week. In the stratosphere, the ECMWF and GFS physics models drive the 60°N 10 hPa wind far below its 1979-2026 record minimum for early November. About 35-51% of ECMWF ENS and GEFS members reverse it briefly, against only 12-14% in the machine-learning AIFS ENS. If the disruption works down, it would raise the odds of a colder, blocked spell from mid-November into early December.

What changed: The main change is that the Met Office has now issued a yellow wind warning covering Lothian for 03:00-21:00 on Tuesday 27 Oct; last run had no warning. The short range is otherwise as expected. This morning is dry and cloudy (airport 9 °C, 1001 hPa). Rain comes around midday, a surge to about 15 °C follows by early evening, and the front arrives in Tuesday's small hours. The hourly guidance now puts Tuesday's gust peak near 80 km/h around 13:00, with 65-75 km/h already around midnight on Monday night, so the central range is now 65-80 km/h. Wednesday also has rain in the small hours. The medium and extended range are unchanged: a strong high from 29 Oct and 1 Nov to about 8 Nov, a changeable mid-to-late November, and blocking returning at 35-45% in early December. In the stratosphere, NASA data is back, confirming the vortex is near its long-term mean now and forecast to fall far below its 1979-2026 record minimum. The Open-Meteo ECMWF ENS series now agrees with the charts (51% of members ever easterly) instead of being discounted. Reversal counts are slightly lower than last run: ECMWF ENS 40-51% (was 44-60%), GEFS 35% (was 45%) and AIFS ENS 12-14% (was 14-22%). GFS now goes deeper, to -5 m/s by 10 Nov, and SSW risk stays medium. The Edinburgh analog winters are now available; they are strong El Niño years with a DJF anomaly of +0.2 °C, mild Decembers and mostly cold Februaries, which supports the existing winter tilt. The severe-weather.eu analog set now includes 2009/10 instead of 1964/65. The self-correction still applies: highs at or slightly above the blend, and clear-night lows shaded down.

SSW risk: medium. A reversal in early November would be almost unprecedented, and even without one the vortex is forecast to be record-weak for the date. The guidance points to a short, shallow event (a few days at 0 to -6 m/s, confined above about 30 hPa) followed by recovery. That lowers the odds of strong downward coupling compared with a deep mid-winter SSW. If it does couple (about two thirds of major events do, typically 1-3 weeks later), the window for Edinburgh is roughly 12 Nov to early December. That fits the AO and NAO dipping negative on 5-9 Nov and the ECMWF extended run bringing blocking back to 35-45% in early December. Coupling would raise the odds of NAO-, northern blocking and colder northerly or easterly spells. In November that mostly means frost and cold nights in the city and snow on the Pentlands and higher ground; lying snow in the city would need a proper northerly or easterly outbreak. The alternative, favoured by the westerly QBO and the ECMWF 46-day rebuild to above normal, is a fast recovery and mild, wet westerlies through much of December. The very strong El Niño keeps a further mid-to-late winter weakening, and a colder-February risk, on the table.

If the disruption couples down (about two thirds of events do, typically 1-3 weeks later), the window for Edinburgh is roughly 12 Nov to early December. That fits the ECMWF extended run bringing blocking back to 35-45% by early December. Coupling would raise the odds of NAO-, northern blocking and colder northerly or easterly spells. In November that mostly means frost and cold nights in the city and snow on the Pentlands and higher ground; city snow would need a proper northerly or easterly outbreak.
